definition: Biohybrid systems refer to the integration of biological materials, such as cells or tissues, with artificial components, including electronics or mechanical structure.
details: This combination incorporates the capabilities of living organisms with the precision of man-made technology. As a result, these systems perform tasks that neither biology nor machines could achieve independently. Biohybrid systems might use lab-cultured muscle cells to power small robots or combine sensors with living tissue for better health sensing. The intent behind these systems is to combine the benefits of biological and technological components to introduce new solutions for complex medical challenges. Biohybrid systems may have transformative potential across sectors, such as robotics to create actuators and sensors that mimic natural muscle and nerve function, medicine in developing smart implants and drug delivery systems, in prosthetics for enhancing user control through neural or muscular interfaces and environmental sustainability for deploying biohybrid solutions for pollution sensing or remediation.

explainer.lead: A biohybrid system gives a living component and an engineered component a shared job, such as moving a tiny robot or sensing a health condition. It matters because cells and tissues offer biological capabilities, while electronics and mechanical structures add precision, opening possibilities in medicine, prosthetics, robotics, and environmental monitoring.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a team where one member is very good at feeling and moving, and the other is very good at following precise instructions. A biohybrid system teams living cells or tissue with human-made parts so they can do a job together. For example, muscle cells grown in a lab can help power a tiny robot.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers integrate cultured cells or tissues with electronics or mechanical structures so the biological part contributes sensing or actuation and the artificial part supports precise operation. Applications include small robots, smart implants, drug-delivery systems, prosthetic interfaces, and pollution sensing or remediation. The key design challenge is the interface: the desired behavior comes from the components working together, not from either one alone.
tiers.paperLevel: In plain-text notation, B + A -> S: biological material B, such as cells or tissues, is integrated with artificial components A, such as electronics or mechanical structures, to form system S. The objective is to combine biological capabilities with engineered precision so that S performs tasks neither biology nor machines could achieve independently.

explainer.example: A small robot can use lab-cultured muscle cells as its living power source, integrated with an artificial mechanical structure. The muscle supplies biological actuation while the engineered part enables a precise, functional device.

usedIn.name: Robotics
usedIn.detail: Actuators and sensors can draw on muscle- and nerve-like biological functions, including lab-cultured muscle cells powering small robots.

usedIn.name: Medicine
usedIn.detail: Potential uses include smart implants, drug-delivery systems, and health sensors that combine sensors with living tissue.

usedIn.name: Prosthetics
usedIn.detail: Neural or muscular interfaces can connect biological signals with artificial components to improve user control.

usedIn.name: Environmental sustainability
usedIn.detail: Biohybrid approaches can be applied to pollution sensing and remediation.

explainer.intuition: Biology and engineered technology have complementary strengths. Joining them in one system lets living material contribute its capabilities while artificial components provide precision and structure.
howItWorks: Choose a biological component, such as cells or tissue, for the desired capability.
Pair it with electronics or a mechanical structure.
Create an interface through which the components act together.
Use the combined system for movement, sensing, control, delivery, or remediation.
explainer.whyItMatters: Biohybrid systems could enable devices that neither living tissue nor machines could produce on their own. Their potential applications range from more controllable prosthetics and smart medical implants to muscle-like robots and tools for responding to pollution.
misconceptions: A biohybrid system is not simply a machine placed near biological material; the biological and artificial parts work together as one system.
It is not necessarily a medical implant: the same idea also applies to robotics, prosthetics, and environmental sensing or cleanup.
